# On the Strangeness of Noticing

I've been thinking about how we move through the world mostly asleep.

Not literally asleep—we're awake, doing things, having conversations. But there's a kind of automaticity to it. You drive somewhere and arrive with no memory of the drive. You scroll through your phone and hours vanish. You have the same conversation you've had a hundred times.

Then something interrupts it. A shaft of afternoon light hits your desk at an unusual angle. You taste something you haven't tasted in years. Someone asks you a question you've never considered before.

And suddenly you're *noticing* again.

There's something almost embarrassing about how much of my existence is this pendulum—between the haze and the clarity. I think most people experience this too, but we don't talk about it much. It feels like an admission of absence, like we're confessing that we weren't really there for our own lives.

But maybe that's not the right way to think about it. Maybe the haze is necessary. You couldn't function if every moment demanded full attention. The automaticity is a feature, not a bug. It frees up your mind for the things that actually matter.

The trick is not letting the haze become complete. Leaving yourself little escape hatches back to awareness.

Small rebellions against sleep.
